title: Even the mind stands on food
hookLine: the ladder climbs past meditation to strength, food and rain, and Hindu homes still honor the food that holds the mind up
last: NAME — THE SELF IS DEEPER THAN NAME AND THOUGHT.

lines: A LADDER FROM BODY TO MIND.
THEN A STRONG ARM, A MEAL, A RAIN CLOUD.
cards: Draw a spiritual ladder, and you'd probably make it climb away from the body: earthy things at the bottom, airy things at the top. Sanatkumara's ladder has been climbing inward: name, speech, mind, will, thought.
Today it reaches meditation, the most inward step yet. Then it does something unexpected. It climbs toward a strong arm, a meal, and a rain cloud.

teach.h: THE EARTH MEDITATES, AS IT WERE.
teach.b: Greater than thought, Sanatkumara says, is meditation, dhyana. The earth meditates, as it were. The sky meditates, as it were.
The waters, the mountains, gods and people, all meditate, as it were. People who achieve greatness, he adds, seem to have a share of it, while small-minded people are quarrelsome and gossiping.
Greater than meditation is understanding, vijnana: by it one knows the Vedas, right and wrong, this world and the next. Then the turn. Greater than understanding is strength.
One strong person can make a hundred people of understanding tremble. The earth stands by strength; the mountains stand by it. Greater than strength is food.
Go without eating for ten days, and even if you live, you can't see or hear or think or understand. Remember Shvetaketu's fast? Same point.
Greater than food is water. When the rains fail, people grow sick with worry about food; when the rains are good, they're glad.

The earth, the sky, the mountains, people, animals, grass and trees, he says, are all water in solid form. So why does the ladder climb into the body? One way to read it: Sanatkumara isn't ranking spirit over matter.
He's asking what each thing depends on.
Understanding on strength; strength on food; food on rain.

teach.h: FOOD, WATER: WHAT HOLDS IT UP?
teach.b: The ladder climbs by asking what holds this up. And at each rung, the same instruction: revere it as Brahman.
Revere food as Brahman. Hindu homes still live by that.

Food is offered before it's eaten, and many families say a verse from the Gita at the table, brahmarpanam: the act of offering is Brahman, what is offered is Brahman. The meal that holds up your mind is treated as holy.
So a rushed lunch at your desk is still, in this teaching, God holding you up. Offering it first is how you notice.

how: Dhyana, meditation, is practiced across Hindu traditions, where it is the seventh limb of Patanjali's eight. Food is treated as sacred: it is offered to God before eating, and many families recite Bhagavad Gita 4.24 (brahmarpanam) as a prayer before meals.

games.why: understanding rests on strength, strength on food. Sanatkumara says revere food as Brahman, so many Hindus offer it before they eat.

practice: Sit for a minute like the mountain, heavy and still, meditating, as it were. Then take a sip of water or a bite of something, but pause first and offer it. If you pray, say brahmarpanam, or simply: this is yours.
If you don't, name what it took: rain, soil, hands. Then eat or drink slowly.

wordCard.voice: Meditation. Dhyana, the rung above thought: the stillness of earth, sky and mountains. Above it, understanding, strength, food and water.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyāna: meditation, steady contemplation. dhyāyatīva pṛthivī: the earth meditates, as it were.

carryVoice: Your line: food is honored as Brahman. Tomorrow, the top of the ladder. Day three hundred fifty-four, done.
